title: Controlling a stage: practices applied and judging the process
blurb: Name the practice a controlling a stage action applies, and decide whether the project manager's stage control is effective, with the reason that fits the scenario.
question: A contractor's site manager agrees a layout change on site and tells the project manager afterwards, who then mentions it in the highlight report. Is the stage being controlled effectively, and which practice should have been applied?

teach.h: Two question types on controlling a stage
teach.body: Practitioner papers ask two things about this process. First, which practice a controlling a stage action applies: the official extracts of table 16.3 that examiners quote cover progress, plans, issues and quality. Second, whether the project manager is controlling the stage effectively: you judge the action against the recommended actions in 16.4, the objectives in 16.2 and the scenario facts, then pick the reason that actually explains the verdict.

teach.h: How controlling a stage applies the practices
head: Practice
What the process does with it (table 16.3)
rows: Highlight reports produced and issued at the frequency the project controls require
Work package descriptions developed or updated; product register, stage plan and project plan updated
Issue management approach applied and built into WPDs; issue register updated
Quality management approach applied and built into WPDs; product descriptions developed or updated
teach.caption: Paraphrased from the official extracts. A WPD can carry quality or issue requirements, so look at WHAT is written into it.

root.label: What did the PM produce or update?

teach.caption: Quality management approach rules written into a WPD apply quality; issue management approach rules apply issues.

teach.body: Good stage control keeps attention on delivering the stage's products, monitors any drift from agreed products and methods so change is never uncontrolled, keeps risks and issues under control, keeps the business case under review, and gets products accepted to the agreed quality, all within tolerance. Check the action against those objectives and the recommended actions, then weigh the scenario facts: team experience, the tolerances set, any tailoring agreed.

teach.h: Signs of effective and ineffective control

rows.label: Escalation
values: Within tolerance, or after the breach

teach.caption: By week 8 only £25k has actually been overspent, but the forecast now passes tolerance. That is the moment to escalate, not when the money is gone.
Within stage tolerance the chain stops at corrective action; the board only sees it in the next highlight report.

teach.body: On the Engineering Skills Centre, the lessons report from an earlier lab refurbishment said contractor progress was only verbal and changes were agreed on site without checking the budget. In the structural works stage, project manager Leah Whitfield writes the quality management approach's inspection rules into each Greystack work package (quality), asks for weekly written checkpoint reports, logs every site request in the issue register before any decision (issues) and keeps the product register and stage plan current (plans). Her highlight reports go to the board fortnightly (progress). That is effective control, shaped by past lessons.

teach.text: Traps: (1) A WPD is a plans product, but writing the issue management approach's rules into it applies the ISSUES practice, and writing quality rules into it applies QUALITY. (2) There is no 'communication practice': highlight reports apply progress. (3) Escalation is triggered by a forecast breach of STAGE tolerance; a work package breach the PM can absorb is handled in the stage. (4) A change agreed on site and reported afterwards is uncontrolled change, however well it is reported.

items: The table 16.3 rows examiners quote for controlling a stage: progress, plans, issues and quality.
Progress: highlight reports at the frequency in the project controls.
Plans: WPDs, product register, stage and project plans updated.
Issues and quality: their approaches applied and written into WPDs; issue register and product descriptions updated.
Judge stage control against 16.2 objectives and 16.4 recommended actions, then pick the reason that fits the facts.

summary: You can now say which practice any controlling a stage action applies, using table 16.3. You can also judge whether stage control in a scenario is effective and choose the reason that explains the verdict, not just a true statement.

A.q: Tarnside College is converting a warehouse into an Engineering Skills Centre. During the structural works stage, project manager Leah Whitfield updates the product register with the status of each product in the stage and revises the work package description for the mezzanine floor after an approved design change. Which practice is the 'controlling a stage' process applying?
A.why: Table 16.3 links controlling a stage to the plans practice through developing or updating work package descriptions and updating the product register, stage plan and project plan.

whyNot.0: Quality is applied when the quality management approach is built into WPDs or product descriptions are updated; here the WPD is revised for a design change.
whyNot.2: Progress is applied in controlling a stage through highlight reports to the board.
whyNot.3: Issues is applied through the issue management approach and the issue register; the approved change is being reflected in the plans products.

A.q: At Tarnside College, Leah Whitfield writes the quality management approach's requirements for building control inspections into each work package description for the structural works, and updates the product description for the fume extraction system with a new airflow specification. Which practice is the 'controlling a stage' process applying?
A.why: Table 16.3: the quality practice is applied when the quality management approach is applied and included in WPDs, and product descriptions are developed or updated.

whyNot.0: WPDs are plans products, but what is written into them here is quality requirements, which applies the quality practice.
whyNot.1: Issues would be applied by writing the issue management approach into WPDs or updating the issue register.
whyNot.3: Progress is applied through highlight reports, not through product descriptions or inspection requirements.

A.q: On the Tarnside project, Greystack's site manager reports that asbestos removal will overrun its work package time tolerance by four days. Leah Whitfield forecasts that the structural works stage can absorb the delay within its time tolerance. What should Leah do next?
options: Raise an exception report to the project board for direction
Ask the board to approve an exception plan for the stage
Tell the site manager to escalate it to the finance committee
Capture the issue, then take corrective action in the stage
A.why: Work-package-level exceptions are handled by the PM in controlling a stage. The issue is registered and assessed, and as the stage can absorb it, corrective action is taken without involving the board (11.2.6, 16.4.5, 16.4.6).

whyNot.0: An exception report is for a forecast breach of stage or project tolerance; this delay fits within stage tolerance.
whyNot.1: Exception plans are prepared in managing a stage boundary after the board responds to an exception report; there is no stage exception here.
whyNot.2: Team managers escalate to the PM, and the finance committee sits in the business layer; neither route fits a delay inside stage tolerance.

B.q: At Tarnside College, Leah Whitfield writes into each Greystack work package description the issue management approach's rules for how site problems and requests for change must be raised with her. Which practice is the 'controlling a stage' process applying?
B.why: Table 16.3: the issues practice is applied when the issue management approach is applied and its requirements are included in work package descriptions.

whyNot.1: The WPD is a plans product, but the content added is the issue management approach's rules, which applies issues.
whyNot.2: Quality would be applied by building the quality management approach into the WPD, not the rules for raising issues.
whyNot.3: Organizing deals with roles and structure; it is not one of the practices table 16.3 links to this action.

B.q: On the Tarnside project, Leah Whitfield sends the project board a highlight report every two weeks, the frequency the project controls require, with a safety section that one governor asked for. Which practice is the 'controlling a stage' process applying?
B.why: Table 16.3: the progress practice is applied when highlight reports are produced and issued at the frequency required by the project controls.

whyNot.0: The board is responsible for the team's safety and well-being, but producing a highlight report is how the progress practice is applied.
whyNot.2: Plans is applied through WPDs, the product register and plan updates, not highlight reports.
whyNot.3: Quality is applied through the quality management approach and product descriptions.

B.q: On the Tarnside project, Leah Whitfield forecasts that the structural works stage will exceed its £60,000 cost tolerance by about £30,000 because more asbestos has been found. Which product should she use to tell the project board?
B.why: A forecast breach of stage tolerance is escalated in escalate issues and risks with an exception report, which sets out options and a recommendation (16.4.7, 11.3.1).

whyNot.0: An issue report records and assesses an issue the PM can handle formally; a forecast breach of stage tolerance needs an exception report to the board.
whyNot.1: The highlight report is the routine time-driven report; the forecast breach needs the event-driven exception report.
whyNot.3: The end stage report is prepared in managing a stage boundary at the end of a stage, not to escalate a forecast breach.

C.q: Greystack hands over the completed mezzanine floor at Tarnside College after passing its own quality checks. The product description names Craig Dunmore, head of estates, as the approver, but Leah Whitfield accepts the floor herself to save time and updates the product register. Is this an appropriate application of the 'receive completed work package' activity, and why?
options: Yes, because the PM receives completed work packages in this activity
Yes, because Greystack has carried out the quality checks in the plan
No, because its product description names a different approver
No, because the project board should approve every completed product
C.why: In receive completed work package, the PM makes sure each product has gained the approval defined in the quality and sustainability responsibilities in its product description (16.4.3). Leah is not the named approver.

whyNot.0: It is true that the PM receives completed work packages, but that does not explain why she can bypass the named approver; she cannot.
whyNot.1: Quality checks are needed, but they do not replace approval by the person named in the product description.
whyNot.3: Approval comes from whoever the product description names; the board does not approve every product.

C.q: Leah Whitfield works on the Tarnside project three days a week. Between Greystack's weekly written checkpoint reports, she holds short informal calls with the site manager to understand emerging problems, and notes the actions they agree in the project log. Is this an appropriate application of the 'evaluate work package status' activity, and why?
options: Yes, because informal talks and checkpoint reviews are both part of it
Yes, because informal calls can replace checkpoints for a part-time PM
No, because agreed actions should be recorded in the issue register
No, because the site manager should report progress to the board
C.why: Evaluate work package status includes informal conversations with the team manager, review of checkpoint reports and, if necessary, updating the project log (16.4.2).

whyNot.1: The verdict is right but the reason is wrong: informal calls supplement checkpoint reports, they do not replace them.
whyNot.2: Formal issues go in the issue register, but noting agreed actions in the project log is a recommended action of this activity.
whyNot.3: Team managers report to the PM through checkpoint reports; the board receives highlight reports from the PM.

C.q: The vice principal for curriculum asks Greystack's site manager for 30 welding bays instead of the 24 in the design. The site manager agrees on site and starts changing the layout, telling Leah Whitfield afterwards, and Leah mentions it in her next highlight report. Is the stage being controlled effectively, and why?
options: Yes, because the highlight report keeps the board informed of the change
Yes, because the senior user controls changes to the user requirements
No, because any change to scope needs an exception plan from the board
No, because the request should be captured and assessed before a decision
C.why: A request for change must be captured and assessed for its impact before a course of action is decided (16.4.5). Agreeing it on site is the uncontrolled change the objectives in 16.2 aim to prevent, and repeats a lesson from the college's last project.

whyNot.0: Reporting the change afterwards does not make it controlled; it was never assessed against cost, time and the business case.
whyNot.1: The senior user does control change to requirements, but here the site manager agreed it without any assessment or authority.
whyNot.2: Changes can be approved by the board or a change authority within the change budget; an exception plan is for forecast tolerance breaches.

reteach.title: Follow the product, then test the action
reteach.question: If you ignore the activity name and look only at the product the PM touched, can you name the practice? And can you test the action against what the activity should achieve?

blocks.body: Which practice: highlight report means progress; WPD, product register or plan updates mean plans; issue register or issue approach rules mean issues; product descriptions or quality approach rules mean quality. Is it effective: did the PM follow the recommended actions, keep change controlled, escalate only a forecast stage breach, and get products approved as their descriptions require?

head: If the action touches...
The practice is
rows: WPD content, product register, stage plan
Issue register, issue MA rules in a WPD
Product descriptions, QMA rules in a WPD

blocks.text: A true statement is not enough. Pick the reason that explains THIS action: 'the PM receives completed work packages' is true, but does not explain whether the right approval was obtained.

explain.h: Plans and progress in the stage
explain.body: Plans: the PM develops or updates work package descriptions and keeps the product register, stage plan and project plan up to date. Progress: the PM issues highlight reports at the frequency the project controls require.

test.q: After the asbestos removal at Tarnside College, Leah Whitfield updates the stage plan and the project plan with actual costs and revised forecasts. Which practice does table 16.3 link this action to?
test.why: Table 16.3 lists updating the stage plan and project plan, with the product register and WPDs, under the plans practice in controlling a stage.

whyNot.1: Progress in controlling a stage is applied through highlight reports to the board.
whyNot.2: Revised costs eventually feed the business case at the stage boundary, but updating the plans applies the plans practice.
whyNot.3: Risk is not the practice linked to updating plans with actuals and forecasts.

explain.h: Issues and quality in the stage
explain.body: Issues: the issue management approach is applied, its rules go into WPDs and the issue register is updated with new issues and actions. Quality: the quality management approach is applied, its rules go into WPDs and product descriptions are developed or updated.

test.q: The nacelle rig manufacturer tells Tarnside College that the rig's foundation pad must carry a higher load. Leah Whitfield updates the product description for the foundation pad with the new load specification. Which practice is the 'controlling a stage' process applying?
test.why: Table 16.3: developing or updating product descriptions in controlling a stage applies the quality practice.

whyNot.0: Plans covers WPDs, the product register and plans; updating a product's quality specification applies quality.
whyNot.2: The change may have started as an issue, but updating the product description is how quality is applied.
whyNot.3: Organizing concerns roles and structure, not product specifications.

explain.body: Effective stage control follows the recommended actions: work packages co-created and accepted, progress gathered from checkpoints and informal talks, new issues registered and assessed before decisions, and products approved by whoever their product descriptions name.

test.q: Paul Kettering, a governor who chairs the finance committee, asks Leah Whitfield for evidence that the structural works stage at Tarnside College is under control. Which observation would best show effective stage control?
options: Every site problem goes straight to the finance committee
Greystack reports progress verbally at weekly site meetings
Completed products carry the approvals in their descriptions
Changes are agreed on site to keep the works moving quickly
test.why: Getting agreed products accepted to the agreed quality is a controlling a stage objective, and receive completed work package checks each product has its requisite approval (16.2, 16.4.3).

whyNot.0: Escalating every problem bypasses manage by exception; only forecast breaches of stage tolerance go to the board.
whyNot.1: Verbal-only reporting was a failing in the college's previous project; checkpoint reports should be written at the agreed frequency.
whyNot.3: Changes agreed on site without assessment are uncontrolled change, which controlling a stage aims to prevent.

explain.body: An exception is a forecast breach of tolerance. The PM escalates when stage or project tolerance is forecast to be exceeded, without waiting for the breach to happen, and does not escalate deviations that can be fixed within stage tolerance.

test.q: At week 8 of the structural works stage at Tarnside College, actual overspend is £25,000, but Leah Whitfield forecasts £65,000 by the end of the stage against a stage cost tolerance of £60,000. What should she do?
options: Wait until the actual overspend passes £60,000
Report the forecast in the next highlight report
Ask Greystack to raise an exception report
Escalate now with an exception report
test.why: An exception exists when a breach of tolerance can be forecast. A forecast breach of stage tolerance is escalated to the board with an exception report straight away (11.2.6, 16.4.7).

whyNot.0: Waiting for the actual breach removes the board's chance to act; exceptions are based on forecasts.
whyNot.1: The highlight report is routine; a forecast tolerance breach needs an immediate exception report.
whyNot.2: Exception reports go from the PM to the board; the contractor's team manager reports to the PM.
